title: Using Codex for an orbital strategy game: the simulation boundary I keep explicit
author: va2k0r
selftext:
I’m developing DeltaV Orbital Strategy with Codex, using TypeScript for the game and Three.js for the 3D view. It’s a turn-based game where the whole fleet shares one fuel reserve, so a movement or an evasion changes what every other ship can afford.

The boundary I keep explicit in the project instructions is that the simulation must run without the browser or renderer. Fleet orders, fuel and combat belong in the core; camera state, lighting and animations do not. An animation finishing should never decide when fuel is deducted or a ship arrives.

A concrete example is ship production. The simulation counts eligible work turns and determines when a ship exists. The assembly sequence only presents that result. That gives me two separate things to check when working with an agent: whether the rules are correct, and whether the 3D sequence actually communicates them. A passing code check doesn’t answer the second question.

The attached trailer shows the current result. I’d like to hear from people using coding agents on games: what boundary or invariant do you put in the project instructions to stop visual work from changing gameplay?

If you want to inspect the playable result, the [free browser tutorial is here](https://deltavorbitalstrategy.com/) (desktop, English and Italian). The full game is a commercial project still in development; this is my own project, hence the self-promotion flair.

comments.author: AetherIndex
comments.body: One of the worst pitches for a game that I've ever heard.
